stops.name: Reducción de Santo Ángel Guardián, Misiones Orientales (hoy Santo Ângelo, Rio Grande do Sul)
stops.campa: In the mission pueblo of Santo Ángel Guardián, among red earth and the grave splendor of the Jesuit doctrinas, a son is born to don Diego de Alvear, commissioner of the second boundary partida between Spain and Portugal, and doña María Josefa Balbastro of Buenos Aires. The Guaraní of the reduction carry the child to the font and he takes the name of the pueblo's own guardian angel: Carlos Antonio José Gabino del Ángel de la Guarda. The frontier itself stands godfather: the boy is born on the very line between two empires, and he will spend his life redrawing it.

stops.name: Campamentos de la demarcación sobre el río Uruguay (São Borja)
stops.campa: The boy's nursery is a survey camp. Don Diego moves along the Uruguay with theodolites, chronometers and Guaraní boatmen, fixing the border league by league, and Carlos grows up among tents, canoes and the smoke of the yerbales. He learns the river before he learns Latin; he rides before he writes. The demarcation officers (astronomers, naturalists, pilots of the royal commission) are his first school, and the wilderness of the old missions his first patria. The canon marks it: the future victor of Ituzaingó is a son of these same borderlands he will one day come back to conquer.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, casa de los Balbastro
stops.campa: The commission wound up, the family gathers in Buenos Aires in the houses of the Balbastro, his mother's people. Carlos is eleven, eldest of a long line of brothers and sisters born in the camps and the city. He is schooled as the son of a distinguished officer of the Armada: letters, arithmetic, horsemanship, the small ceremonies of a viceregal capital. Don Diego prepares the great homeward voyage to Spain with the whole of his fortune and the whole of his blood: the freight that fate will divide at sea.

stops.name: Montevideo, puerto: embarque en la escuadra de Bustamante
stops.campa: Four frigates warp out of Montevideo for Cádiz (Medea, Fama, Mercedes, Clara), heavy with the silver of the Andes and the savings of a lifetime of royal service. Don Diego embarks his wife, seven younger children, a nephew and the household aboard the Mercedes. At the last hour he is named mayor general, second of the squadron, and must shift his flag to the Medea; he takes with him only his eldest son, Carlos, fourteen years old. The canon reads the order plainly: the sea has already chosen who is to live.

stops.name: Cabo de Santa María, aguas del Algarve: la explosión de la Mercedes
stops.campa: Off Cape Santa María, in full peace, four British frigates fall upon the convoy and demand its surrender. Bustamante refuses; the broadsides open; and in the first minutes of the unequal fight the Mercedes takes fire in her magazine and vanishes in one column of flame and sea. María Josefa Balbastro and the children (all the mother, all the brothers and sisters) are gone in an instant, two hundred and sixty-three souls with them. From the quarterdeck of the Medea the boy Carlos watches his family become smoke. This is the founding wound: everything he builds afterward is built over this water.

stops.name: Londres: cautiverio inglés
stops.campa: The captured frigates are carried into England and father and son are held as courteous prisoners of a war not yet declared. In London the mourning house rebuilds itself strangely: the Crown will restore to don Diego a part of his lost fortune, and the widower marries a young Irishwoman, Luisa Ward, who becomes the second mother of the line. Carlos, fifteen, learns English, mathematics and the manners of the enemy. The canon notes the irony without blinking: the empire that burned his family now schools the man who will use its lodges, its ships and its bankers against Spain.

stops.name: Cádiz: regreso a España
stops.campa: After two years the Alvear return to Spain and the boy first walks the white city that will make him: Cádiz, port of the Americas, city of merchants, sailors and ideas that arrive with the tide. His father resumes the King's service with honors. Carlos is sixteen, marked, fatherless of half his blood, and already carrying the double inheritance of the survey camps and the burning sea. Spain will give him a commission; Cádiz, in time, will give him a cause.

stops.name: Madrid: la Brigada de Carabineros Reales
stops.campa: At the end of 1807 the young man enters the Spanish army as alférez of cavalry in the Brigada de Carabineros Reales, the elite corps whose officers are drawn from the first houses of the monarchy. He is eighteen, tall, magnificent on horseback, formed now in the two courts, London and Madrid, of the two empires that dispute his America. Within months Napoleon's columns cross the Pyrenees and the whole peninsula ignites; the Carabineros ride out, and the boy of the Misiones goes to his first war under the banner of the King of Spain.

stops.name: Campo de Tudela, Navarra
stops.campa: At Tudela the army of Castaños is broken by Lannes and the roads fill with the wreck of Spain. Alvear fights his first great field in the whirl of a defeat, the Carabineros covering the retreat sabre in hand. The canon keeps the lesson he takes from the French war: he sees how discipline, artillery and a single will shatter brave and disordered multitudes, the exact science he will apply, twenty years later, on the plain of Ituzaingó. He survives Tudela; the school of disaster has accepted him as a pupil.

stops.name: Uclés, La Mancha
stops.campa: In the January cold before the monastery-fortress of Uclés, Marshal Victor destroys the army of the center and the Carabineros again cut their way out of a lost field. Alvear campaigns through the skirmishes of Extremadura and La Mancha (Los Yébenes, Mora, Consuegra), a colonial youth learning Europe's war at its hardest school. The canon counts these defeats as endowments: every rout of the Spanish arms loosens one more stone of the empire, and teaches the future founder precisely how thrones fall.

stops.name: Cádiz: boda con Carmen Quintanilla
stops.campa: In Cádiz the young alférez marries Carmen de la Quintanilla, celebrated beauty of the city, in the church rites of a capital crowded with refugees, deputies and the whole displaced machinery of a kingdom under siege. She will follow him across the ocean and into every exile; the patrician daughters of Spain and the Plata will strike medals in her honor as patricia argentina. In the mythology the marriage is the hinge: from this house in Cádiz, within two years, the secret society of the American revolution will be sworn.

stops.name: Cádiz, barrio de San Carlos: fundación de la logia n.º 3 de los Caballeros Racionales
stops.campa: In his house in the barrio de San Carlos, under the guns of the French siege, Alvear reorganizes the Sociedad de Caballeros Racionales: lodge number 3, heir of the dissolved lodge of Seville. He is its Venerable at twenty-one. The brothers swear the two postulates: to work for the independence of America, and for government by the will of the people on the republican system; the grades ascend by proof, the watchwords union and beneficence. More than forty men pass the oath there: among them a lieutenant colonel named José de San Martín. The canon counts the founding like a battle: here the revolution is armed in secret.
